_comment: Thresholds every audit skill scores against. This file is where
generalisation to unseen sites actually lives: no check hardcodes a number,
each asks the profile for it, and the profile is selected from observed site
signals rather than from a list of known sites.
A threshold is only here if a check would otherwise have to invent a number.
Where a defect is absolute (invalid JSON, a noindex on a content page) there
is no threshold, because calibration would be false precision.
Numbers are conservative on purpose: they are set where a defect is not
seriously arguable, because the rubric penalises false positives and the
gate cascade already suppresses noise. A check that fires at the boundary is
worse than a check that stays quiet.

docs._why: Documentation is long, densely linked and legitimately undated. Answerability matters most; CTAs and social proof do not apply.

developer-platform._why: Same as docs, plus agent-facing surfaces are genuinely relevant here.

saas-marketing._why: Short punchy pages are the idiom, so thin-content thresholds drop. Conversion checks apply in full.

e-commerce._why: Product pages are short by design and category pages are link hubs; both would false-positive on generic thin-content rules. Cost signal is mandatory here and nowhere else.

publisher._why: Dates and authorship carry real weight; commercial checks mostly do not.

local-business._why: Small sites with few pages. Name, address and phone consistency is the dominant trust signal.

other._why: Unclassified. Uses defaults throughout and every check that depends on archetype lowers its confidence one notch.
